title: JOHN D'ANGELICO / AN ARCHTOP GUITAR, STYLE NEW YORKER, NEW YORK, 1961
description: JOHN D'ANGELICO / AN ARCHTOP GUITAR, STYLE NEW YORKER, NEW YORK, 1961 / The headstock inlaid D'Angelico New York New Yorker, stamped internally D'Angelico New York 2136, length of back: 21 7/16 in. (54.4 cm) with original case and soft case (4)
lot_essay: Sold with original bill of sale, John D'Angelico, New York, August 26, 1961 This guitar has remained in the possession of the original owner since 1961, when it was purchased directly from John D'Angelico. As a young man, the owner studied guitar in Allentown, Pennsylvania, under the tutelage of a guitar teacher who happened to own two D'Angelico New Yorkers. After getting the address from his teacher, the owner traveled to D'Angelico's shop on Kenmare Street in New York, and put down a deposit for a New Yorker with a natural finish. When the owner went to D'Angelico's shop several months later to make his final payment on the guitar, he spied another New Yorker in a red sunburst finish on the workbench, and informed D'Angelico that he would prefer the same red finish for his new guitar. D'Angelico speedily obliged the request to change the finish, and the owner took possession of the guitar shortly thereafter.

description: GIOVANNI BAPTISTA GUADAGNINI / A VIOLIN, PIACENZA, CIRCA 1740 / Labeled JOANNES GUADAGNINI fecit Placentiae anno 1740, length of back: 13 15/16 in. (354 mm) with case (5)
provenance: It would appear to the casual observer that Giovanni Battista Guadagnini was a violin maker with a touch of wanderlust. Having worked in Piacenza, Milan, Parma and finally Turin, he developed a distinctive style based on his interpretations of the work by Antonio Stradivari. The results were violins that are tonally superior to many of his contemporaries. Guadagnini's early pieces from Piacenza represent works from a violin maker whose craft is already firmly developed. His masterful and individualistic style-seen here in the signature oval shape of the F holes' lower lobes and the undercutting on the volute-illustrate a maker who was very quick and deft in his tool handling skills. His illustrious red varnish, both brilliant and transparent, is of a quality that could incite jealousy in any contemporary maker.
